title: xView2 machine-learning damage maps may have been used by UN INSARAG teams in Adıyaman and by AFAD, the World Bank, IFRC and WFP after the 6 February 2023 Türkiye earthquakes
summary: MIT Technology Review (20 February 2023), quoting DIU: xView2 used by two UN INSARAG teams in Adıyaman and by AFAD, World Bank, IFRC and WFP; Microsoft reports 3,849 damaged buildings mapped for AFAD.
account: MIT Technology Review reported on 20 February 2023 on xView2, an open-source building-damage assessment project. It was sponsored and developed in 2019 by the Pentagon's Defense Innovation Unit (DIU) and Carnegie Mellon University's Software Engineering Institute. Partners included Microsoft and UC Berkeley. It uses machine-learning (semantic segmentation) on satellite imagery to identify and grade building damage. Ritwik Gupta, DIU's principal AI scientist, told the magazine about use in Türkiye. At least two ground teams of search and rescue personnel from the UN's International Search and Rescue Advisory Group (INSARAG) had used xView2 in Adıyaman. He said it helped workers find damaged areas they were unaware of. He said AFAD, the World Bank, the IFRC and WFP had all used the platform. Atishay Abbhi, a World Bank disaster risk management specialist, said the same degree of assessment would typically take weeks and now takes hours or minutes. The article notes that the first usable satellite images came on 9 February 2023, three days after the first quake. It says the model is up to 85 or 90% accurate. Microsoft's February 2023 “Turkey Earthquake Report” has authors including Gupta and Microsoft AI for Good staff. It states that the team partnered with AFAD to deliver building-level damage estimates over four cities in southeast Türkiye. The imagery was from the first three days. It estimated 3,849 buildings damaged or destroyed, with Marash the most affected at 7.44% of buildings. The World Bank GRADE report does not mention xView2, AI or Microsoft. DLR's peer-reviewed account states its own AI damage products were not part of the viewer delivered to responders. Direct Relief's December 2025 article describes a research study on Microsoft and Google models rather than a response decision. The MIT Technology Review article's publication date is used. No responder statement describing a decision taken on xView2 output is among the sources.
purpose: Rapid building-damage assessment from pre- and post-event satellite imagery for humanitarian assistance and disaster response. This use was that purpose.
system: xView2 building damage assessment models (semantic segmentation on satellite imagery, trained on the xBD dataset)
developer: US Defense Innovation Unit (DIU) with Carnegie Mellon University Software Engineering Institute; research partners Microsoft AI for Good and UC Berkeley
deployer: UN INSARAG (search and rescue ground teams in Adıyaman); AFAD, World Bank, IFRC and WFP (per the developer's account); Microsoft AI for Good delivered estimates to AFAD (per Microsoft)
location: Adıyaman and four cities in southeast Türkiye including Kahramanmaraş (Marash)
taxonomy_note: Loose fit; the responder-use claim rests on the developer's account relayed by one news item and Microsoft's own report.

ratings.reason: No individual rescue or beneficiary is attributed to the maps in any source on file.

Responders are reported to have received building-level damage maps in hours instead of weeks and to have found damaged areas they were unaware of. The reports come from the developer and a World Bank specialist, not the responding agencies.
No downstream effect on rescues, shelter siting or reconstruction is documented. The maps covered part of the affected zone after imagery became usable on 9 February.

ai_role.statement: The AI produced the damage classifications that responders are said to have used. Which decisions changed is not documented. Sources: the developer (DIU's Gupta) and the World Bank specialist, quoted in one news report, and Microsoft's own report of delivering estimates to AFAD. World Bank's GRADE report and DLR's account do not corroborate operational use of AI products.

produced_by: Usable high-resolution post-event satellite imagery (first available 9 February 2023, three days after the quake)
A pre-trained open-source damage model (xBD/xView2) run by the developers on request of responding organizations
Direct contact between DIU/Microsoft researchers and responders (UN INSARAG teams, AFAD)
must_hold: Cloud-free daytime imagery with a satellite overhead. The article notes far fewer images in remote or less developed areas such as Syria
Responder trust in an off-site AI product, which the developer describes as hard to obtain
Documentation by the responding agency of what the maps changed, which no source on file provides

echoes.setting: Earlier deployments by the California National Guard and the Australian Geospatial-Intelligence Organization for wildfires and after flooding in Nepal, per the same MIT Technology Review article; no outcomes documented
Research study by Direct Relief and Stanford assessing health-facility damage with Microsoft AI for Good and Google models for the 2023 earthquakes (not an operational use)

headline: UN INSARAG teams in Adıyaman may have used xView2 damage maps

comparator.quote: this same degree of assessment would typically take weeks and now takes hours or minutes

later.note: Direct Relief's 10 December 2025 article describes a retrospective research study of the Microsoft and Google 2023 models that found they disagreed in significant ways; no later operational use of xView2 was found in the sources read and web search was unavailable.
